# Sanitizing Log Output

This example demonstrates a common secure-coding problem: sensitive data can
leak through logs even when the application logic itself appears harmless.

Logging is a data sink. If untrusted or sensitive values are written to logs
without review, the leak is often durable, widely replicated, and hard to
clean up afterward.

The preferred outcome is to avoid logging sensitive values at all. The
techniques in this example are compensating controls that reduce exposure
when risky log statements already exist or when multiple call sites feed the
same logging pipeline.

The example uses Logback with SLF4J to show two mitigation strategies:

- deny the entire log event when it contains a suspicious value
- keep the event but mask the sensitive substring before it is rendered

The regexes in this example are intentionally small and illustrative. They are
good enough to explain the mechanism, but not sufficient as a production-grade
payment-data detection strategy.

## What you will learn

By the end of this example you will understand:

- why logs are part of your application's data-leak surface
- how to recognise a baseline log statement that should not reach production logs
- how a Logback filter can deny an entire event before it is written
- how a custom message converter can mask only the sensitive portion of a log line
- why deny-vs-mask is a policy choice with real trade-offs

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 21 or newer](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java21)

This example uses the Maven Wrapper (`./mvnw`), so you do not need to install
Maven separately.

Run all commands in this walkthrough from this example directory:
`examples/sanitizing_log_output`.

## Build the example

Build the project once before running the walkthrough.

We use `package` here because the example produces a shaded jar, which keeps
the run commands simple while we swap Logback configurations externally.

What you gain from this step: one repeatable artifact for all three logging
modes.

```shell
./mvnw clean package
```

Build output

```
...
[INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS
[INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
...
```

## Inspect the baseline application

Start with the application code.

The Java logic is intentionally tiny so the lesson stays focused on logging,
not on business behavior. Two log statements contain data that resembles a
payment-card number. One uses hyphens and one is a plain sixteen-digit string.

What you gain from this step: you see exactly what data the logger receives
before any sanitization is applied.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.logs;

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

/**
 * Demonstrate some sensitive data logging.
 */
public final class App 
{
    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(App.class);

    public static void main( String[] args )
    {
        log.info("Here's an innocuous log statement.");
        log.info("captured card number 4403-9999-8888-7777 expiration 0126");
        log.info("captured card number 4406999988887777 expiration 0126");
        log.info("All done!");
    }
}
```

## Run the baseline configuration

Run the application with the default Logback configuration.

We do this first so the problem is concrete: the log sink currently receives
the full sensitive values unchanged.

What you gain from this step: a clear baseline showing the leakage.

```shell
java -cp target/sanitizing_log_output-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar com.oracle.jsc.logs.App
```

Observed output

```
20:40:56.877 [main] INFO  com.oracle.jsc.logs.App -- Here's an innocuous log statement.
20:40:56.879 [main] INFO  com.oracle.jsc.logs.App -- captured card number 4403-9999-8888-7777 expiration 0126
20:40:56.880 [main] INFO  com.oracle.jsc.logs.App -- captured card number 4406999988887777 expiration 0126
20:40:56.880 [main] INFO  com.oracle.jsc.logs.App -- All done!
```

The problem is obvious in the output:

- the formatted credit-card-like values are logged verbatim
- the unformatted sixteen-digit value is also logged verbatim

This is exactly the kind of issue teams miss when they think only about
databases or HTTP responses and forget that logs are another output channel.

## Inspect the deny strategy

The first mitigation uses a Logback filter.

A filter runs before the event is emitted. If the message matches one of the
suspicious patterns, the filter returns `DENY`, and the whole log event is
dropped.

What you gain from this step: you see the strongest of the two mitigations and
exactly where the policy decision is made.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.logs;

import java.util.regex.Pattern;

import ch.qos.logback.classic.spi.ILoggingEvent;
import ch.qos.logback.core.filter.Filter;
import ch.qos.logback.core.spi.FilterReply;

public final class SanitizingFilter extends Filter<ILoggingEvent> {

    private static final Pattern CC_NUMBER_PATTERN = Pattern.compile("\\d{4}-\\d{4}-\\d{4}-\\d{4}");
    private static final Pattern SIXTEEN_DIGITS_PATTERN = Pattern.compile("\\d{16}");

    @Override
    public FilterReply decide(ILoggingEvent event) {
        String message = event.getFormattedMessage();

        if (CC_NUMBER_PATTERN.matcher(message).find() ) {
            return FilterReply.DENY;
        }
        if (SIXTEEN_DIGITS_PATTERN.matcher(message).find() ) {
            return FilterReply.DENY;
        }
        return FilterReply.ACCEPT;
    }

}
```

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE configuration>

<configuration>
    <appender name="STDOUT" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder class="ch.qos.logback.classic.encoder.PatternLayoutEncoder">
            <pattern>%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS} [%thread] %-5level %logger{36} -- %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
        <filter class="com.oracle.jsc.logs.SanitizingFilter" />
    </appender>

    <root level="debug">
        <appender-ref ref="STDOUT" />
    </root>
</configuration>
```

This strategy is simple and strong:

- if the event looks dangerous, do not write it
- there is no risk of partially masking the wrong substring

The trade-off is that you lose the entire event, including any benign context
around the sensitive value.

## Run the deny strategy

Run the same application again, but tell Logback to use the filter-based
configuration.

What you gain from this step: you see the effect of dropping risky events
entirely.

```shell
java -Dlogback.configurationFile=src/main/resources/logback-filter.xml -cp target/sanitizing_log_output-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar com.oracle.jsc.logs.App
```

Observed output

```
20:40:57.111 [main] INFO  com.oracle.jsc.logs.App -- Here's an innocuous log statement.
20:40:57.113 [main] INFO  com.oracle.jsc.logs.App -- All done!
```

The sensitive lines are gone completely.

That is often the safest default when the value is not needed for operations.
If a log event is risky and nonessential, denying it is usually better than
trying to preserve it.

## Inspect the masking strategy

The second mitigation keeps the event but rewrites the sensitive fragment.

Logback's pattern layout renders `%msg` using a message converter. This example
replaces the normal `%msg` converter with a custom one that masks the matched
values before the line is written.

What you gain from this step: you see how to preserve operational context while
still reducing disclosure risk.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.logs;

import java.util.regex.Pattern;

import ch.qos.logback.classic.pattern.MessageConverter;
import ch.qos.logback.classic.spi.ILoggingEvent;

public final class PatternLayoutSanitizingEncoder extends MessageConverter {

    private static final Pattern CC_NUMBER_PATTERN = Pattern.compile("\\d{4}-\\d{4}-\\d{4}-\\d{4}");
    private static final Pattern SIXTEEN_DIGITS_PATTERN = Pattern.compile("\\d{16}");

    @Override
    public String convert(ILoggingEvent event) {
        return sanitize(super.convert(event));
    }
    
    private String sanitize(String msg) {
        String out = msg;
        if (CC_NUMBER_PATTERN.matcher(out).find()) {
            out = CC_NUMBER_PATTERN.matcher(msg).replaceAll("xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx");
        }

        if (SIXTEEN_DIGITS_PATTERN.matcher(out).find()) {
            out = SIXTEEN_DIGITS_PATTERN.matcher(out).replaceAll("xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx");
        }

        return out;
    }
}
```

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE configuration>

<configuration>
    <conversionRule conversionWord="msg" class="com.oracle.jsc.logs.PatternLayoutSanitizingEncoder" />

    <appender name="STDOUT" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder class="ch.qos.logback.classic.encoder.PatternLayoutEncoder">
            <pattern>%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS} [%thread] %-5level %logger{36} -- %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

    <root level="debug">
        <appender-ref ref="STDOUT" />
    </root>
</configuration>
```

This strategy keeps more context than the deny approach:

- the event is still visible in the log stream
- the sensitive substring is replaced with marker characters

The trade-off is that masking logic must be correct and consistently applied.
If the pattern misses a case, the data can still leak.

## Run the masking strategy

Run the application again with the masking configuration.

What you gain from this step: you can compare preserved context against the
stricter deny approach.

```shell
java -Dlogback.configurationFile=src/main/resources/logback-mask.xml -cp target/sanitizing_log_output-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar com.oracle.jsc.logs.App
```

Observed output

```
20:40:57.347 [main] INFO  com.oracle.jsc.logs.App -- Here's an innocuous log statement.
20:40:57.349 [main] INFO  com.oracle.jsc.logs.App -- captured card number xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx expiration 0126
20:40:57.349 [main] INFO  com.oracle.jsc.logs.App -- captured card number xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx expiration 0126
20:40:57.349 [main] INFO  com.oracle.jsc.logs.App -- All done!
```

The result keeps the surrounding message but removes the sensitive value:

- `4403-9999-8888-7777` becomes `xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx`
- `4406999988887777` becomes `xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx`

This is useful when the event itself still has operational value and you do
not want to drop the entire line.

It is still weaker than removing the sensitive value at the source, because
the masking rule has to recognise every format you consider dangerous.

## What this example teaches

- The best fix is to avoid logging sensitive values in the first place.
- Logs are an output channel and must be treated as part of your data-protection boundary.
- A filter can block an entire risky event before it is written.
- A masking converter can preserve context while reducing disclosure.
- Deny and mask are both valid patterns, but they solve different operational needs.
- Regex-based sanitization is only as good as the patterns and policy behind it.
